title: HEC-RAS 2D Flood Modeling with Claude (Lee County, Iowa)
context: Rainfall-runoff modelling is used to estimate the watershed response to rainfall by converting precipitation to runoff and into river discharge. HEC-HMS can simulate different hydrological processes included in rainfall-runoff process like precipitation losses, runoff transformation, baseflow, and river routing. Developing a rainfall-runoff model requires several spatial and time-series datasets, and observed river discharge can be used to evaluate how accurately the model represents the actual watershed response. The model creation is likely to be challenging for AI and the assessment of model results by AI will be even more interesting.
occupation: PhD Student Hydraulics and Hydrological Engineer with

session_goal_achievement.Why or why not: The AI agent was able to assist partially in getting data and setting up model. The main drawback is that if it makes one mistake, until the user does not point out the correct issue, AI is likely to move in circles, testing every issue except the one that is causing the problem.

Step 1.step_name: Download DEM and rainfall data for creating the model
Step 1.step_action: Identify a US location with high-quality 1m DEM and rainfall data, download the DEM tile, and locate matching NOAA rainfall data.

nodes.label: Ask Claude for a US location with 1m DEM + rainfall data
nodes.detail: Participant opened a new Claude.ai chat and asked for a US location with at least 1m resolution DEM and available rainfall data, stating the goal was to run a flood model in HEC-RAS.

nodes.label: Research and recommend a test watershed
nodes.detail: Claude web-searches USGS 3DEP 1 m DEM coverage and NOAA Atlas 14 rainfall availability and recommends Ellicott City, Maryland (Tiber-Hudson watershed) as a small-catchment test bed, with links to the DEM and rainfall sources.

nodes.label: Check the link and request exact DEM download steps from OpenTopography
nodes.detail: The participant opens the link Claude provided, then shares the OpenTopography raster page for the USGS 1 m DEM and asks Claude for exact steps to download it.

nodes.label: Walk through OpenTopography download workflow
nodes.detail: Claude explains that this dataset is gated to academic accounts and walks through the OpenTopography raster job form (area of interest, product, GeoTIFF format) with step-by-step download instructions.

nodes.label: Ask for steps to interact with the website
nodes.detail: The participant asks Claude for steps to interact with the OpenTopography website.

nodes.label: Give website interaction steps and a bulk-download shortcut
nodes.detail: Claude gives the steps for using the site and points out the Bulk Download link as a shortcut if the account gate blocks access.

nodes.label: Download DEM tile and share with Claude for validation
nodes.detail: The participant selects the National Map downloader link from Claude's Route B, ticks the 1 m DEM product in the TNM Downloader, downloads an Iowa tile (x60y452), and uploads it to the chat, asking Claude to check whether it is adequate and to give a rainfall data link for the same location.

user_response.label: reject
user_response.reasoning: ignore the recommendation of ellicott city

user_response.label: adopt
user_response.reasoning: follow claude's route b and download the dem from national map

nodes.label: Inspect DEM quality and flag coverage gaps
nodes.detail: Claude reads the raster's metadata, statistics, and extent with rasterio, renders a hillshade preview, and reports that the file is a valid 1 m DEM but this tile is 76% empty (nodata) because of a county-line boundary.

nodes.label: Clarify study is a generic test, not a site-specific flood study
nodes.detail: Participant clarified the HEC-RAS study was a random test of the flood modeling workflow rather than a site-specific engineering study, simplifying downstream requirements.

nodes.label: Accept the tile for a test run and crop a clean window
nodes.detail: Claude says the tile is fine for a learning run and crops a 2.0 x 3.5 km window with no nodata cells (27 m relief, native 1 m, EPSG:26915), sharing it as a test clip.

nodes.label: Check the cropped test clip and its download link
nodes.detail: The participant opens the cropped test-clip preview and its download link; by this point the participant has also downloaded a second tile for the same location from a different 3DEP project (IA_SouthCentral_2020) in the TNM Downloader.

nodes.label: Request beginner-friendly NOAA rainfall download steps
nodes.detail: The participant asks for brief steps to download rainfall data from the NOAA website, noting zero familiarity with the site.

nodes.label: Walk through NOAA Atlas 14 PFDS download
nodes.detail: Claude walks through the NOAA Precipitation Frequency Data Server, explaining that the key value is the 100-year 24-hour depth to be spread with a temporal distribution.

nodes.label: Ask for the abbreviation of Iowa
nodes.detail: While following the NOAA steps, the participant asks Claude what the abbreviation of Iowa is.

nodes.label: Answer that Iowa's abbreviation is IA
nodes.detail: Claude answers that the two-letter postal abbreviation is IA, which is also what PFDS uses and what appears in the DEM filename.

nodes.label: Ask for the specific county and location within Iowa
nodes.detail: The participant asks Claude to be specific about which county and location within Iowa the DEM covers.

nodes.label: Pinpoint the county and location of the DEM
nodes.detail: Claude reverse-geocodes the DEM's valid-area centroid, identifies northwest Lee County, Iowa (with nearby townships, drainage, and the USGS 3DEP project details), and explains that the void is a county-line boundary.

nodes.label: Locate the site on the NOAA PFDS map while Claude works
nodes.detail: While Claude pinpoints the location, the participant looks up Lee County on the NOAA PFDS map and starts typing the next request.

nodes.label: Review Claude's location details
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's location write-up (Lee County, drainage, survey credentials).

Step 2.step_name: Model Setup: Create geometry, mesh and boundary conditions
Step 2.step_action: Set up the HEC-RAS project, terrain, 2D flow area, mesh, and boundary conditions with Claude's guidance.

nodes.label: Share a second/replacement DEM tile and request full HEC-RAS setup steps
nodes.detail: Participant uploaded a different .tif for the same location (avoiding the void issue) and asked Claude for comprehensive but brief steps to build the rainfall-runoff model in HEC-RAS.

nodes.label: Analyze new DEM and merge/catchment options
nodes.detail: Claude inspected the second DEM tile, checked overlap with the first, and offered to merge them or delineate a catchment; it installed pysheds and ran flow accumulation to delineate a candidate catchment boundary and shared a preview image.

nodes.label: Create terrain in RAS Mapper while Claude analyzes the DEM
nodes.detail: While Claude inspects the new DEM, the participant opens RAS Mapper and creates a new RAS terrain from the DEM, then starts typing the next instruction.

nodes.label: Stop the generation and reject merging the DEMs
nodes.detail: Participant told Claude not to merge the DEMs and to use only the new DEM tile for the flood model, redirecting the catchment delineation.

user_response.label: reject
user_response.reasoning: stop claude generation and reject mergeing two dem

nodes.label: Deliver 10-step HEC-RAS geometry/mesh/BC setup guide
nodes.detail: Claude gave a step-by-step guide covering units (SI, UTM Zone 15N/NAD83/NAVD88), project setup, terrain creation, 2D flow area, mesh, Manning's n, rainfall assignment, boundary conditions, and plan/run steps; it flagged that a 15m mesh would be coarse relative to the 1m DEM.

nodes.label: Review Claude's HEC-RAS setup guide
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's 10-step HEC-RAS geometry, mesh, and boundary-condition guide.

nodes.label: Open HEC-RAS, create the project, and follow the instructions
nodes.detail: Participant opened HEC-RAS 6.6 and RAS Mapper, created the project AI.prj, and attempted to add layers before a project was fully initialized, then set the project properly.

nodes.label: Ask about appropriate mesh size for a 1m DEM
nodes.detail: Participant asked Claude what mesh cell size to use given the 1m DEM resolution and what units to set in HEC-RAS.

nodes.label: Recommend SI units and mesh size trade-off
nodes.detail: Claude confirmed the DEM was in meters (EPSG:26915, UTM 15N/NAD83, NAVD88) and instructed the participant to set HEC-RAS to SI units before building anything, warning that leaving it on US Customary units would corrupt all depth/velocity/discharge outputs by a factor of 3.28.

nodes.label: Follow the instructions, create terrain, 2D flow area, mesh, and boundary conditions in RAS Mapper
nodes.detail: The participant builds the terrain from the DEM in RAS Mapper, draws a rectangular 2D flow area (rather than importing Claude's catchment boundary), generates the mesh, and sets Normal Depth boundary condition lines on all sides of the flow area.

user_response.label: modify
user_response.reasoning: adopt claude's steps but with some differences

Step 3.step_name: Setting up unsteady flow conditions and computational settings
Step 3.step_action: Configure the rainfall hyetograph, unsteady flow boundary/simulation window, and computational settings, then run the simulation.

nodes.label: Request 5-min 10-year rainfall event for unsteady flow input
nodes.detail: Participant asked Claude to use the downloaded NOAA rainfall data and derive a 5-minute 10-year event for the unsteady flow input.

nodes.label: Compute the 5-min 10-year rainfall depth
nodes.detail: Claude computes the 5-minute 10-year depth (0.691 in = 17.6 mm, 90% CI 14.5-21.3 mm) and notes that such a short burst will barely activate the channel network, suggesting a longer simulation window.

nodes.label: Ask for normal depth and computational settings for a short run
nodes.detail: The participant reads the answer and asks Claude, based on the DEM, what the normal depth should be and what computational settings to use for a short model run.

nodes.label: Provide the normal-depth slope and computational settings
nodes.detail: Claude measures the friction slope along the main channel near the outlet (0.004) for the normal-depth boundary condition and gives computational settings for a short run.

nodes.label: Ask which HEC-RAS settings specifically need to change
nodes.detail: The participant reviews the earlier responses and asks Claude for only the HEC-RAS settings that need to be changed from the defaults.

nodes.label: List the non-default settings to change
nodes.detail: Claude lists only the settings that must be changed in HEC-RAS (in a Where / Setting / Default / Change-to table), saying to leave everything else alone.

nodes.label: Review the settings to change
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's table of settings to change.

nodes.label: Ask for 10-minute rainfall
nodes.detail: The participant asks for the 10-minute rainfall, saying they want to run 10-minute data.

nodes.label: Deliver the 10-minute duration rainfall row
nodes.detail: Claude interprets the request as a 10-minute storm duration and gives the 10-minute row from the participant's Atlas 14 table.

nodes.label: Set boundary conditions and enter the 10-minute rainfall in HEC-RAS
nodes.detail: The participant sets the Normal Depth boundary conditions in the Unsteady Flow Data editor and enters Claude's 10-minute rainfall into the precipitation hydrograph table.

nodes.label: Point out that no curve number (CN) was added
nodes.detail: The participant tells Claude that no curve number / infiltration has been added.

nodes.label: Confirm the run can proceed without infiltration
nodes.detail: Claude says that is fine for this run: with no infiltration layer, HEC-RAS treats every cell as impervious and all 25.7 mm becomes runoff.

nodes.label: Ask for computational settings
nodes.detail: The participant reads the reply and asks Claude for the computational settings.

nodes.label: Specify the simulation window and computational settings
nodes.detail: Claude gives the unsteady flow analysis window (a 5-hour simulation), computation interval, and output intervals.

nodes.label: Enter computational settings, test-run, and create a smaller test geometry
nodes.detail: The participant enters the computational settings in the Unsteady Flow Analysis window (with a much shorter simulation window than Claude suggested), runs a first computation, and then draws a new, smaller 2D flow area in RAS Mapper to cut the runtime.

user_response.label: modify
user_response.reasoning: adopt the computation and intervals. cut the simulation window and shrink area (modification)

nodes.label: Launch the unsteady flow simulation
nodes.detail: Participant started the HEC-RAS unsteady flow computation using the simplified geometry, rainfall boundary, and configured computational settings.

Step 4.step_action: While the model computes, determine what to check, then share and analyze the depth/velocity results against the DEM-derived channel network.

nodes.label: Ask what logs/metrics to check while HEC-RAS computes
nodes.detail: While the simulation ran in the background, participant asked Claude what parameters or metrics could be used to assess the model results once finished.

nodes.label: Enumerate result-checking options (logs, hydrographs, rasters)
nodes.detail: Claude listed available diagnostics: computational log volume-accounting/errors, stage-flow hydrographs, rating curves, cell hydrographs, profile lines, and depth/velocity raster outputs, explaining how to interpret each.

nodes.label: Check the HEC-RAS computation and review Claude's list
nodes.detail: The participant checks the HEC-RAS computation window and reads Claude's list of result checks.

nodes.label: Paste the computational log to Claude
nodes.detail: The participant pastes the HEC-RAS computational log into the chat.

nodes.label: Confirm the solver is healthy and outline next checks
nodes.detail: Claude confirms the solver is healthy (0.45% volume accounting error, completed cleanly) and outlines what can be checked next.

nodes.label: Check the computation and review Claude's response
nodes.detail: The participant checks the HEC-RAS computation and reads Claude's response.

nodes.label: Say they want a short run
nodes.detail: The participant tells Claude they want it to be a short run.

nodes.label: Point out the run took two seconds
nodes.detail: Claude notes the run took only 2 seconds at 633x real time, so extending the simulation to 5 hours would cost about 30 seconds.

nodes.label: Rerun in HEC-RAS and send the computational log
nodes.detail: The participant works in HEC-RAS on the small test area and sends Claude the new computational log, noting a small area was used.

user_response.label: reject
user_response.reasoning: ignore claude, keep shrinking the area

nodes.label: Give feedback on the computational log
nodes.detail: Claude confirms precipitation is working correctly and the mass balance closes, and says the remaining problem is only that the run is too short.

nodes.label: Review the feedback and ask what can be checked in the results
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's feedback and asks (several times, after a cut-off reply) what can be checked in the results.

nodes.label: Give a full inventory of what can be checked
nodes.detail: Claude gives the complete inventory of RAS Mapper layers, hydrographs, and other outputs that can be checked.

nodes.label: Share depth/velocity rasters and VRT files for analysis
nodes.detail: Participant uploaded the resulting max-depth and max-velocity GeoTIFF/VRT raster files (having already shared the flow hydrograph for one boundary condition) and asked Claude to evaluate them.

user_response.label: adopt
user_response.reasoning: follow claude list to export results and send back to claude for comparison

nodes.label: Run D8 flow accumulation and compare modeled flood extent to DEM channel network
nodes.detail: With context near 95%, Claude clipped the source DEM to the model extent, derived a D8 flow-accumulation channel network, and statistically compared it to the wet cells from the HEC-RAS results, generating a network_comparison.png overlay figure. Claude concluded 'the network matches well where the model has water; failure is coverage, not location,' citing a median offset of 1.0m and 96% of deep cells within 10m of the DEM channel centerline, while noting only ~24% of the DEM network was wet due to the short simulation window.

nodes.label: Work in RAS Mapper while Claude analyzes the rasters
nodes.detail: While Claude analyzes the uploaded rasters, the participant keeps working in RAS Mapper.

nodes.label: Review Claude's response about running D8 flow accumulation and compare modeled flood extent to DEM channel network
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's comparison of the modeled flood extent against the DEM-derived channel network ('the network matches well where the model has water; the failure is coverage, not location').

Step 5.step_name: Feedback on how to improve the model and its results
Step 5.step_action: After the session resumes, get and discuss concrete recommendations for improving the model, then receive a final summary of the whole workflow.

nodes.label: Ask how to improve the model without heavy time/compute cost
nodes.detail: After the session resumed, participant asked Claude how the model could be improved without spending a lot of time or computational resources.

nodes.label: Deliver ranked, cost-annotated improvement recommendations
nodes.detail: Claude gave a ranked list of improvements with estimated runtime cost: extend the simulation window to 3 hours, fix output intervals, add missing boundary condition lines, use spatially varied Manning's n from NLCD land cover, refine mesh only on valley floors (5m vs 15-20m), add breaklines along thalwegs at 5m spacing, run a longer/larger 6-hour 100mm storm, clip the 2D area to a real catchment boundary, add SCS-CN infiltration, and run a mesh convergence check at 20/15/10m.

nodes.label: Review the recommendations and ask whether the results are acceptable
nodes.detail: The participant reads the ranked recommendations and asks for Claude's point of view on whether the results are acceptable.

nodes.label: Distinguish model validity from result acceptability
nodes.detail: Claude answered that 'the results are not acceptable as they stand, but the model is,' clarifying that the physics/mesh setup was sound but the short simulation window, disabled infiltration, and rectangular (non-catchment) domain limited how the current results should be used.

nodes.label: Push back that 30 minutes is enough to reach the hill bottom
nodes.detail: The participant argues that 30 minutes is enough time for rainfall to reach the bottom of the hill, even if not the downstream boundary.

nodes.label: Concede the point and correct a wrong number
nodes.detail: Claude agrees water did reach the valley bottoms, corrects one of its earlier numbers, and revises its explanation.

nodes.label: Argue the '76% dry' figure may mean water already drained
nodes.detail: The participant argues that the '76% dry' network could also mean the rain stopped and water already left the cells for the stream network.

nodes.label: Test the dry-channel explanation and revise the verdict
nodes.detail: Claude explains a maximum-depth raster cannot show drained cells, re-tests whether dry channels were time-limited or clustered, admits the 24% recall figure was untrustworthy, and narrows its criticism.

nodes.label: Request a minimum-change action list for analysis and discussion
nodes.detail: The participant asks for the minimum changes to improve and use the current result, as brief points usable in an analysis and discussion write-up.

nodes.label: Give a 3-edit minimum-change list plus a full model summary
nodes.detail: Claude gives three near-zero-cost fixes (confirm rainfall depth vs. intensity units, extend the end time, tighten output intervals) followed by points for the analysis and discussion (terrain and setup, numerical performance, network validation, routing evidence, limitations).

nodes.label: Review the summary and clarify the hydrograph covered only one boundary condition
nodes.detail: The participant reads the summary and clarifies that the flow hydrograph shared earlier was for only one boundary condition.

nodes.label: Recompute boundary/outlet locations and correct prior volume claims
nodes.detail: Claude located all DEM channel crossings along the model boundary with their contributing areas and terrain elevations, corrected two earlier claims (a BC elevation comparison and an unpeaked-hydrograph inference), and gave a revised per-boundary volume breakdown for the participant to verify against RAS Mapper.

nodes.label: Review Claude's corrected boundary and outlet analysis
nodes.detail: The participant reads Claude's corrections and its table of where DEM channels cross the model boundary.
